chunks: "A square wave is a periodic signal that sits at one of two voltage levels and flips between them, spending exactly half of each period at each level.
So it has an amplitude, a period or frequency, and a 50% duty cycle. If the duty cycle isn't 50% I'd call it a rectangular wave or a pulse train.
The numbers I care about: for a wave swinging between 0 and V, the average is V/2 and the RMS is V over root two, about 0. 707 volts.
If it's symmetric around zero, plus and minus A, the average is zero and the RMS is just A, because it's always at magnitude A. The part I find most useful is the frequency view.
A square wave contains only odd harmonics, the fundamental plus 3f, 5f, 7f and so on, with amplitudes falling as one over n.
The fundamental of a plus-minus A wave has amplitude 4 amps over pi, about 1. 27 amps. An ideal square wave has instant edges, which means infinite harmonics.
Real ones have a finite rise time, which limits the content and sets how much high-frequency energy actually shows up as ringing, crosstalk and EMI.
So I think of a square wave as a time-domain shape with an edge-rate knob, and that knob is what I'd manage on a board."
